range_summary: Southern Canada, nearly all of the contiguous US (excluding the southwestern deserts), south to Venezuela and Bolivia.

Circumboreal. Most of Canada and Alaska, south to British Columbia, Montana, Wyoming, Oklahoma, Missouri, Ohio, Virginia and along the Appalachians; range has expanded south in the Great Plains since the mid-1960s.
Much of the western United States, including the Channel Islands of California, and the Baja Peninsula.

notes: Named only inside generic skunk classes

range_summary: Southwestern US south to northern Nicaragua. In the US: southeastern Colorado, extreme northwestern Oklahoma, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas.

range_summary: Western North America north to southern Oregon, northern Nevada, northern Utah, southern Wyoming and Colorado, south through California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas into Mexico; old records from Kansas.

Historically the central plains from southern Alberta and Saskatchewan to northern Texas, including southern Manitoba; present range is much restricted, nearly continuous from Wyoming south through eastern Colorado, western Kansas, the Oklahoma Panhandle and eastern New Mexico.
Southeastern Oregon, Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, southern California, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas, south to central Mexico.

Much of the western US and part of southwestern Canada, including California, Nevada, Oregon, Washington, Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, Idaho, Montana, South Dakota, Alaska (Kuiu and Admiralty islands) and British Columbia.

Central Arizona, southwestern New Mexico and southern Texas south through Mexico and Central America; occurrences farther north in Arizona/New Mexico likely wanderers or released captives. Texas status uncertain.
notes: Arizona source bot-blocked

From the Bighorn Basin in southern Montana across central and southwestern Wyoming into western and north-central Colorado and eastern Utah.
Central Colorado to central Arizona, including part of southeastern Utah and much of northwestern New Mexico.
Northern Great Plains: southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, Montana, North Dakota, northeastern South Dakota, western Minnesota and northwestern Iowa.

Central Rocky Mountains from southeastern British Columbia and southwestern Alberta south through northern and eastern Washington, northeastern Oregon, northern and central Idaho and western Montana; mainly 700-8,000 ft.

Southern Montana, southeastern Idaho, western Wyoming and north-central Utah.

Alaska, Yukon, mainland Northwest Territories and northern British Columbia; ADW gives the west coast of Hudson Bay to western Alaska.
South-central Canada to Texas, and from Montana, Wyoming, Utah and eastern Arizona to Michigan, Ohio, Missouri and Oklahoma.
Southeastern Nevada, Utah, Colorado and extreme western Oklahoma south through the southwestern US into Mexico; sea level to 2,900 m.
South-central British Columbia and southern Alberta south to southern California, Nevada, southern Utah and northern New Mexico, typically above 2,000 m.
Alaska to Yukon and Northwest Territories, south to northeastern Washington, central Idaho and western Montana.
Lake Chelan and Tacoma, Washington south through Oregon, western Nevada, and the Sierra Nevada and coast ranges of California to Baja California.
Central and southeastern Arizona, west-central New Mexico and northeastern Sonora, Mexico.
Southwestern British Columbia south through the coast ranges, Cascades and Sierra Nevada to southern California and northern Baja California.
Alaska and Canada south to northern California, Colorado, Michigan, Wisconsin, North Carolina and Tennessee, with isolated high-elevation populations.
Eastern North America from Quebec south through the eastern United States (source gives Quebec to Honduras overall).
Northern and western Alaska (also eastern Siberia).
Native to Europe and western/central Asia. Introduced to North America (southern Ontario, Great Lakes, northeastern US, from 1893-1912).
Native to the Iberian Peninsula and Mediterranean; introduced worldwide, including established populations in North America.
Southeastern US: southeast Virginia, southern Georgia, eastern Alabama, Florida peninsula and coastal islands; largest population in the Great Dismal Swamp.

range_summary: Great Basin and intermountain West: southwestern Montana through southern Idaho, Oregon, northern Utah, Nevada, eastern California, with isolated populations in Washington and Wyoming.
notes: Closed where audited

range_summary: Central and southeastern Alaska, Yukon-Tanana uplands, Richardson Mountains (Yukon/NWT) and northwestern British Columbia.
South and Central America into the southern US, expanding north since the 1800s to Missouri and Illinois.
Native to India and Pakistan. The ADW page does not describe North American introduced populations.
Formerly across the Northern Hemisphere; in North America now largely western. Introduced to Ireland, Argentina, Chile, Australia and New Zealand.
notes: Distinct from elk, Cervus canadensis

range_summary: Native to southern Africa; successfully introduced to the southwestern US and Mexico.
Native from Turkey and the Caucasus east to Iran, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan. In North America, introduced to the Florida Mountains near Deming, New Mexico in 1970.
Feral populations occur on islands worldwide, including Hawaii and California's San Clemente Island; NatureServe records the species (Capra hircus) as present in Hawaii, New Mexico and California.

European mouflon originate from Corsica and Sardinia. In North America DLNR lists mouflon sheep and mouflon-feral hybrid sheep on Hawaii Island and mouflon on Lanai; Wikipedia says it is kept on game ranches in Texas and has been introduced to Hawaii.
notes: The European mouflon; authorities differ on whether it is a wild species or feral domestic sheep (Ovis aries musimon)

range_summary: Domestic sheep are established worldwide as introduced animals. DLNR lists feral sheep and mouflon-feral hybrid sheep on Hawaii Island (Mauna Kea); NatureServe records Ovis aries in Wyoming and Hawaii.

Domestic worldwide. The sources read document feral populations mainly outside North America (New Zealand, islands); CDFW discusses escapes and case studies in the US but does not describe an established North American feral population.
Brooks Range of northern Alaska, perhaps also northern Yukon (unconfirmed).
Southwestern British Columbia south along the Cascade, Olympic, Coast and Siskiyou ranges to central California and the Sierra Nevada.
North-central California and west-central Nevada south to Baja California.
Native from India to southeastern China and the Malay Peninsula. Introduced and established in California, Texas and Florida (and Australia and New Zealand). Not native to Canada.

Native to the Himalaya from Kashmir through northern India to Nepal and Sikkim, and southern Tibet. Introduced in New Zealand, California and South Africa (NatureServe); Animal Diversity Web also lists New Mexico and Ontario.
notes: undefined

range_summary: In the US, NatureServe records the species in Nevada (introduced); Audubon calls its U.S. range limited.
Extreme southern Texas (Rio Grande Valley) south through Mexico and Central America; NatureServe also records it in Georgia.
Native to southern Asia; first brought to Hawaii in 1962 as a gamebird. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.

Native to Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and smaller Japanese islands; introduced populations in Hawaii are reported stable; introduction to mainland North America was unsuccessful, and it has been crossed with common pheasants on some North American game farms.
notes: Treated as a species by Hawaii's rules and most checklists; some authorities fold it into the common pheasant

range_summary: Native to East Asia; domesticated since about the 13th century. NatureServe records it in Hawaii; Hawaii DLNR lists it among Hawaii's game birds.
Native to India; introduced to Hawaii. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.
Native to India; introduced to Hawaii in 1959. NatureServe records it in Florida.
Native to Ethiopia and Sudan; introduced to Hawaii in 1957. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.
notes: Hawaii rules call it Erckel's francolin

range_summary: Introduced to Hawaii Island by the Nevada game department as a trial for possible import to Nevada. NatureServe records it in Hawaii.
Native across most of sub-Saharan Africa. In Hawaii, domestic-type birds have been released and live in open urban fields near ponds and wetlands.
Native to southern Europe. The Wikipedia page says the name 'rock partridge' has been used in the US for several Alectoris species and hybrids, so North American records may not be this species.
Native to France, Iberia and northwest Italy; naturalised in England and Wales. The page read does not describe North American populations.
Native to Asia; introduced from Asia to Hawaii in the 1800s and to California. NatureServe records it in California, Utah and Hawaii.

Native from southern Thailand and the Malay Peninsula to Sumatra and Java. Introduced to Hawaii in 1922 and now on all main islands, where it is one of the most abundant birds; established on other Pacific and Indian Ocean islands. Not established on the North American mainland in these sources.
notes: Hawaii rules call it barred dove

range_summary: Permanent resident from northern Mexico and southern Texas (lower Rio Grande Valley) south to southern Brazil, Uruguay and eastern Argentina.
Native to Eurasia; introduced and established throughout most of the world, including across North America.

Two natural resident ranges: the western Gulf Coast from Alabama west to Texas and south to Tamaulipas, and the Florida peninsula. Populations introduced from the 1970s exist in eastern Georgia and eastern South Carolina.

Breeds from southeastern Arizona, southern New Mexico and west-central Texas south into the Mexican highlands. Non-breeding birds occur casually north through much of Colorado and Utah; accidental in California, Wyoming and Nebraska.
notes: Split from mallard by the AOS in 2020

range_summary: Resident from southern Arizona and southeastern Texas south through Middle and South America; possibly expanding into eastern Texas and southwestern Louisiana; small flocks may wander well north of the normal range.

Breeds in southern California, southwestern Arizona, central and eastern Texas, Gulf Coast Louisiana and locally southern Florida, south to central Mexico; also breeds in Hawaii (Oahu) and in South America, Africa and India. Spread east along the Gulf Coast from about 1950.

Wild birds are native from northeastern Mexico south to South America, with small numbers on the Rio Grande in southern Texas. Most Muscovies in North America are barnyard-type birds, and U.S. records probably pertain to escapes or unsuccessful introductions (NatureServe).
notes: Native in south Texas; feral elsewhere

range_summary: Breeds in Eurasia. In North America winters on the Pacific coast from southeastern Alaska to northern Baja California and on the Atlantic-Gulf coast from Labrador and Newfoundland to Florida and southern Texas.
notes: Regular visitor; taken under general duck bags

range_summary: Native to sub-Saharan Africa and the Nile Valley. Escaped birds have established wild populations in Florida (largest), Texas and California, mostly in urban and suburban areas.

More than 90 percent of the breeding population nests in the eastern Bering Sea region of western Alaska (Kuskokwim Bay to Kotzebue Sound), with small numbers in eastern Asia. Most winter in the Aleutian Islands; autumn strays reach Oregon and California.
Coasts of the western Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean: Massachusetts south through Florida along the Atlantic, and Florida west to Tamaulipas along the Gulf.

Breeds from southeastern Bering Sea and southern Alaska and from southern British Columbia east through Manitoba to coastal Quebec and Newfoundland, south to Baja California, the Gulf Coast, Florida and Belize; breeding range has expanded.

In North America breeds along the Atlantic coast from the Gulf of St. Lawrence and southwestern Newfoundland to Nova Scotia (recolonized Maine); winters from the breeding range south to North Carolina, sometimes farther. Also Iceland, southwestern Greenland and much of the Old World.

Breeds on islands and coasts in the Arctic of North America and Eurasia, south to the Aleutians and Kodiak, Hudson Bay and the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Newfoundland waters are the most important western Atlantic wintering area; regular in winter off New England.

Breeds along North Pacific coasts from the Bering Strait south to central California and the North Atlantic from western Greenland and Iceland south to Newfoundland; some birds reach New England waters and southern California in winter.

Resident from northernmost North America south to southern Baja California, Nicaragua and Texas, and east of the Rockies to southern Saskatchewan, northeastern Minnesota, northern Michigan and southern New England; also Greenland, Iceland and the Old World.
Resident from south-coastal and southern Alaska through western Canada to eastern California, southern Nevada and Utah, northern New Mexico and western Kansas and Oklahoma.
Native to Eurasia; introduced in New York City in 1890. Now breeds from southeastern Alaska across southern Canada and south through most of the U.S. to southern Mexico.
Native to the Old World; introduced and established from the north coast of British Columbia and southern Yukon to Newfoundland and south beyond North America.
Breeds from southern Yukon across Canada to Nova Scotia and south through the U.S. and Central America to Costa Rica; winters over much of the U.S., especially the south.

Breeds from central-interior British Columbia east to extreme western Ontario and northwestern Ohio, south to southern California, New Mexico and northern Texas; winters from central California, Arizona and Texas south into Mexico.

Breeds from central interior British Columbia to the western Great Lakes, south to northwestern Baja California, Nevada, Texas and northern Iowa; present year-round in parts of the western U.S. and winters east to the southeastern U.S. and Mexico.

Breeds from Alaska to Labrador and south to central British Columbia, northern Great Lakes, Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine and Nova Scotia; in the non-breeding season ranges south to Texas, the Gulf Coast and northern Florida, primarily the southeastern U.S. Assessed Special Concern in Canada.
notes: A declining species; current federal depredation coverage not verified

range_summary: Breeds from southeast Alaska, northern British Columbia and southern Mackenzie to Newfoundland, south to central Mexico, the Gulf Coast and southern Florida; winters from the northern U.S. south.
Resident from extreme southeastern California, Arizona, southwestern New Mexico and western and southern Texas south to Panama; northern populations partially migratory.
Resident from eastern Panama south to central Chile and Argentina; expanded through the Caribbean during the 1900s, reaching Puerto Rico in 1955; in North America occurs mostly in southern Florida.

Breeds from northeastern British Columbia and southern Mackenzie to Newfoundland, south to southern Texas, the Gulf Coast and southern Florida, west to Wyoming, Colorado and New Mexico; winters from Kansas, the southern Great Lakes and New England south.

Resident from southeastern California and southern Nevada east to southern Nebraska and southwestern Missouri, south into South America; breeding range is expanding, with recent nesting in Oregon and probably Idaho.

Coastal eastern US from Long Island and New Jersey south through peninsular Florida and west along the Gulf coast to southeastern Texas; absent from the western Florida Panhandle. Not a Canadian species.

Breeds in Arctic Russia and in Alaska (Arctic Coastal Plain and Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta); Alaska and eastern Siberian birds molt and winter mainly along the Alaska Peninsula; some Russian-Atlantic birds winter in Europe.
notes: Federally threatened; closed in Alaska

range_summary: Breeds in Arctic Alaska (Beaufort Sea west to Norton Sound and the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta) and eastern Russia; non-breeding in the Bering and Chukchi seas.
notes: Federally threatened; closed in Alaska

range_summary: Breeds on Arctic tundra from Alaska and northern Canada to Labrador; many winter on the northern Great Plains and Prairies, with irregular southward irruptions.
notes: Alaska names a resident season; its federal basis is unresolved

range_summary: Pacific coast from the Bering Strait and Alaska south to Baja California, including British Columbia; northernmost breeders move south in winter.
notes: Alaska names a season; its federal basis is unresolved

range_summary: Native to India and southeastern Asia. Small semi-domesticated populations are introduced and established in scattered North American localities and Hawaii.
Sporadic introduced colonies near Los Angeles, in southern Florida and in Illinois.
notes: Domesticated form of the African collared-dove

range_summary: Coastal North Carolina to the Florida Keys, west to southern Texas, north to southeastern Oklahoma and Arkansas. Not native to Canada.
Native to northeastern India east through southern China and Southeast Asia and the Malay Peninsula. Established in the Florida Everglades (first nest found in 2006). Not native to Canada.

Native to Brazil, Paraguay, Bolivia, Uruguay and Argentina. Breeding populations in Florida (Hillsborough, Miami-Dade and Charlotte counties per FWC); NatureServe lists Florida and Georgia as established and possibly South Carolina. Not native to Canada.

Native from Central America through tropical South America and some Caribbean islands. Introduced in southern Florida (mostly the southern half of the peninsula, commonest near the coast), Puerto Rico and Hawaii. Not native to Canada.

East of the Rockies from the Canadian border to the Gulf and Atlantic; in Canada mainland Nova Scotia, southern New Brunswick, southern and central Québec and Ontario, southern Manitoba and southeastern Saskatchewan. Introduced in the western US and Canada.
Montana to southern Québec, south to northern Mexico and the Florida panhandle, with introductions elsewhere. In Québec it is concentrated around Lake Champlain and its tributaries.
Native from Michigan to Argentina, east of New Mexico. Established outside its range in many areas including Florida, New York and New Mexico; Animal Diversity Web also lists Canada.
notes: Native in the south-central US; introduced elsewhere

range_summary: Central New England to northern Florida, west to eastern Texas, central Oklahoma, eastern Kansas, southeastern Nebraska, Iowa and southeastern Minnesota; spotty at the western and northern edges. NatureServe ranks it NX (presumed extirpated) in Canada.

Southern New England to northern Florida, west through the southern Great Lakes states and southern Iowa to southeastern Nebraska, eastern Kansas, eastern Oklahoma and eastern Texas. Not a Canadian species.
Southern Alberta and southern Saskatchewan south to northern Mexico, west to Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado and extreme eastern Arizona, east to the Dakotas, Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas.
Southern British Columbia south to central Baja California and east to the Rocky Mountains.
Native from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and southern Québec west to the Great Lakes and south through most of the central and eastern US to northeastern Mexico; widely introduced in the west.
notes: Introduced and invasive in the west

range_summary: Eastern United States and adjacent southeastern Canada. Introduced in Newfoundland, British Columbia, Washington and Utah.

Great Slave Lake, Hudson Bay and Labrador south to southern New England, Kentucky, Nebraska, New Mexico and Arizona, west to southeastern British Columbia and eastern Washington/Oregon; spotty and partly introduced in the west.

Southern South Dakota to central Texas, west to eastern Colorado and eastern New Mexico, east to Indiana and southeastern Missouri; disjunct in southeastern Arizona. Hybridizes with northern leopard frog in eastern Colorado and Nebraska. Not a Canadian species.
Western North America from eastern British Columbia and western Alberta south through the western United States to California, Arizona and New Mexico, at roughly 1,220-3,965 m.
notes: undefined

range_summary: Pacific coast from extreme southeastern Alaska through coastal British Columbia, Washington and Oregon to northern California (Mendocino area), from sea level to about 3,110 m.

Southern Canada south through much of the western and central United States to central Mexico; absent from most of the Great Basin and the far western US west of the Rockies, where it has been introduced in many localities. Meets the eastern tiger salamander's range in the Great Plains.

Eastern and central North America; Animal Diversity Web describes the broadly defined tiger salamander as ranging from southeastern Alaska to southern Labrador and south across the US to the Mexican Plateau, a range that includes forms NatureServe now assigns to other species.
Pacific coast from southern Alaska to Baja California and east through the Rocky Mountains to west-central Alberta, Montana, Wyoming, Utah and Colorado; absent from most of the desert Southwest.

Great Plains, southwestern US and northern Mexico: from southern Manitoba and southeastern Alberta south to central Mexico; east to western Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri and Oklahoma, west to central Montana, Colorado and southeastern California.

California, Nevada, central Utah, Colorado and southwestern Kansas south to southern Baja California and Querétaro, Mexico, at elevations up to about 1,980 m. Not reported from Canada in the sources read.

Central and southwestern United States from southern Texas to northern Montana and North Dakota and west across the desert Southwest to Utah, with isolated populations in Idaho, Washington, Oregon and California; adjacent northern Mexico.
Coastal forests of Oregon and northern California, from the Columbia River south, plus a separate group on Vancouver Island and adjacent islands in British Columbia; sea level to about 1,500-1,700 m.

Southwestern Oregon south through the California coastal mountains to the Russian River (Sonoma County), with isolated populations near Santa Cruz and around Shasta Lake; sea level to about 1,700 m. Not found in Canada.

California Coast Ranges from Humboldt County into Baja California, the central Sierra Nevada foothills, and offshore islands (South Farallon, Santa Catalina, Los Coronados); sea level to about 5,000 ft.

Humid coastal forests of northern California (Del Norte to Sonoma County) and, in Canada, Vancouver Island, adjacent small islands and one Sunshine Coast location in British Columbia; absent from Oregon and Washington.
Central and southern California, southern Nevada, southern Utah, Colorado, southern Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas, south into Baja California and Mexico; not in Canada.
Oregon and Idaho south through California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Colorado and western Texas to Baja California and northern Mexico.
Colorado Plateau and vicinity in southern Utah, western Colorado, northern Arizona and northern New Mexico at about 1,200-2,440 m; introduced and established at Cove Palisades State Park, Oregon.

Coastal southwestern Oregon south through coastal northern California and the Coast Ranges to the Monterey Bay lowlands and Tres Pinos Creek area (Santa Cruz and San Benito counties), plus parts of the inner Coast Ranges; not in Canada.
Southern California from the base of the San Gabriel and San Bernardino mountains south to El Rosario, Baja California, plus Catalina and offshore islands; up to about 1,500 m. Not in Canada.

Deserts of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico: northwestern Nevada and southwestern Utah south through southeastern California, Arizona and extreme southwestern New Mexico to Baja California and Sinaloa; sea level to about 1,520 m. Not in Canada.

Southern British Columbia and Alberta south to west-central California, central Nevada and southern Utah; Pacific coast east to north-central Wyoming and western Montana. Distribution is patchy, especially at southern and eastern edges.
Mojave, Sonoran and Colorado deserts of southern California, southern Nevada, northwestern Arizona, Baja California and northwestern Sonora, below about 1,400 m in California.

Only turtle spanning North America coast to coast: from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick across southern Canada to Vancouver Island, and through most of the eastern and central US to the Gulf Coast in Louisiana; a few isolated populations occur in the southwest US and Mexico.

Southern California, southern Nevada, southwestern Utah, western and southern Arizona and extreme southwestern New Mexico, and throughout Baja California and western Sonora; from below sea level to about 2,000 m. Not in Canada.

Southern British Columbia, southern Saskatchewan, southern Ontario and southern Maine south through most of the United States (to southern California, Arizona, Texas and Florida) and into Mexico, Guatemala and Belize.
Southern United States from North Carolina and Florida west through Kansas and southern Nebraska to Arizona and California (to San Francisco Bay), and north-central Mexico; not in Canada.

California from the Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges through southwestern California to northwestern Baja California; up to about 1,835 m in California. The Alameda striped racer subspecies is restricted to the Coast Ranges east of San Francisco Bay. Not in Canada.

Southeastern Washington and southern Idaho south through Oregon, eastern California, Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico and western and central Texas into northern Mexico; up to about 3,077 m.
Outer Coast Ranges of northern California and southwestern Oregon, the Klamath Mountains, and parts of the southern Oregon Cascades; parapatric with C. tenuis in places. Not in Canada.

Southern Vancouver Island and Gulf Islands (British Columbia) south through Washington, Oregon and northern California, including the Sierra foothills; in Washington it occurs in about thirteen disjunct areas.

Southeastern California, central and southern Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas south into Mexico; in Nevada only the far southern tip (NDOW) and rare in far southeastern California (CDFW). Kansas records may be translocated animals (NatureServe).

Southeastern California, southern Nevada and extreme southwestern Utah south through southwestern Arizona into northeastern Baja California and northwestern Sonora; from below sea level to about 1,830 m (NatureServe).

Northern half of the Baja California Peninsula north into southern California, southern Nevada, western Arizona and southwestern Utah (NatureServe); in Nevada a small range in the southeast, overlapping the Panamint rattlesnake near Las Vegas (NDOW).
Southern California, southern Nevada and southwestern Utah south through Arizona, southern New Mexico and western Texas into central Mexico; sea level to about 2,530 m (NatureServe).
Part of southern California (not the southernmost part) and adjacent southwestern Nevada (NatureServe); overlaps the southwestern speckled rattlesnake in parts of the Las Vegas Valley (NDOW).
Southeastern Oregon and southern Idaho south through northeastern California, Nevada, and western and central Utah to southeastern California and western Arizona (NatureServe).

Southeastern Utah, southern Colorado, Kansas and central and southern Missouri south through Arizona, New Mexico, western and central Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas into northern Mexico; Louisiana records may not be natural (NatureServe). Missouri populations north of the Missouri River appear introduced (MDC).

Desert slopes of the Peninsular Ranges in southern California north to the San Jacinto Mountains near Palm Springs, and much of Baja California; an isolated Tecate Mountain (San Diego County) population needs confirmation (NatureServe; theNAT).
Coast to coast across North America; northern limit of the continuous range reaches Nova Scotia, southern Quebec and southern Ontario, and it occurs disjunctly in the West (NatureServe).
Extreme southwestern British Columbia (Chilliwack River drainage) south through western Washington and Oregon to northwestern California (NatureServe).

Southern Nevada, southern California east of the Sierra Nevada and Coast ranges, and western and central Arizona south through Baja California and Sonora; United States range closely matches that of creosote bush; below sea level to about 1,520 m (NatureServe).

Southern British Columbia including Vancouver Island, south through western Washington and Oregon to west-central coastal California and the central Sierra Nevada, and in the Rockies to northern Idaho and western Montana, with disjunct populations in south-central Oregon, northeastern California and northwestern Nevada (NatureServe).
Mainly west of the Cascade-Sierra Nevada crest from south-central Washington through western Oregon and California to northern Baja California; introduced at Las Vegas, Nevada (NatureServe).

Southwestern British Columbia south along the Coast Ranges to northwestern Baja California, and on the western slopes of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada; absent from the Sacramento-San Joaquin valley; sea level to about 8,000 ft (NatureServe). North of the Sunshine Coast it is known from only a few isolated sites in British Columbia (BC).

Oregon, southern Idaho, Utah and western Colorado south through eastern and southern California, Nevada, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas to northeastern Baja California and north-central mainland Mexico (NatureServe).

Introduced in North America. Native to the Mediterranean region and nearby (NatureServe; NDOW); established from Florida to Texas and north into southeastern states, in Arizona and southern California, and in southern Nevada urban areas (NatureServe; NDOW).
Southern South Dakota to central Texas, southwest to southeastern Utah and Arizona, and south to Jalisco and Guanajuato, Mexico (NatureServe).

Western and southeastern Colorado and southern Utah south through Arizona and western New Mexico into Mexico, with isolated populations in northeastern New Mexico and the Big Bend area of Texas (NatureServe).

South-central British Columbia south through Washington, Oregon, southern Idaho, eastern California, Nevada, Utah and western Colorado to Arizona, northeastern Baja California and northwestern mainland Mexico (NatureServe).
Northern California south through western California to southern Baja California (NatureServe).
Southern Oregon, western and southern Nevada, southern Utah and extreme southwestern Colorado south through California and Arizona to southern Baja California and northern Sinaloa (NatureServe).

Utah, eastern Montana, South Dakota and Nebraska south through parts of Wyoming, Colorado, Kansas and Oklahoma to southeastern Arizona, southern New Mexico, southern Texas, southern Arkansas and Louisiana west of the Mississippi; to about 2,740 m (NatureServe).

Discontinuous from east-central Nevada and central and western Utah south to near (mostly north of) the Mogollon Rim in Arizona and New Mexico (NatureServe); in Nevada limited to east-central mountains (NDOW).

Western United States: around the Central Valley of California along the Sierra Nevada and Northern Coast Ranges, north into the Klamath Mountains in Oregon, with a disjunct population in the Columbia Gorge in Washington; populations south of Monterey Bay are treated as L. multifasciata by NatureServe (NatureServe).

San Diego County, California, along the coastal Peninsular Ranges, north into the Mohave Desert and east in the Sonoran Desert of California and western Arizona (north of the Gila River), plus the Newberry Mountains in southern Nevada (NatureServe).

Native to extreme southern New Mexico and central and western Texas south through eastern and southern Mexico to Nicaragua; introduced and well established in the Imperial Valley and along the lower Colorado and Gila rivers in California and Arizona, replacing native lowland leopard frogs (NatureServe).

Lowlands of the southeastern United States from southern New York to the Florida Keys, west to eastern Kansas, central Oklahoma and eastern Texas; introduced on Little Bahama Bank. Not reported for Canada in the source.

Nova Scotia west across southern Canada (Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba) to southeastern Saskatchewan, south through the northeastern and Midwestern US to Virginia, Missouri, Nebraska, New Mexico and Utah; western populations are highly disjunct.

Southwestern Illinois, Missouri, southern South Dakota and southeastern Colorado south to San Luis Potosi and Veracruz, through most of Texas, with a disjunct population in eastern Utah and western Colorado. Not found in Canada.

From San Gorgonio Pass (Riverside County, California) south through the Peninsular Ranges to at least Bahia de los Angeles in Baja California, plus some Gulf of California islands; in the US limited to eastern San Diego and central Riverside counties, to about 1,200 m.

Eastern Washington south to northeastern California and east to northern Nevada and eastern Idaho; an old record exists from extreme southwestern Montana. Historical records near Osoyoos Lake, British Columbia, but considered extirpated from Canada.

Southeastern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan south through eastern Montana, the western Dakotas, Wyoming, western Nebraska, Colorado, Utah, eastern Nevada, New Mexico, Arizona and western Texas to northern Mexico; limits around southeastern Idaho, northern Utah and Nevada are not precisely known.

Southeastern Oregon, southwestern Idaho and northern Utah south through eastern and southern California, Nevada and western Arizona to northeastern Baja California; from below sea level to about 1,980 m.

Southern California (north to Inyo County), southern Nevada, extreme southwestern Utah and central Arizona south to southern Baja California and southern Sonora, Mexico; in Nevada only the south of the state; below sea level to about 1,220 m.
Southern British Columbia, southern Alberta, southern Saskatchewan, Minnesota and Indiana south through most of western and central North America to northern Baja California, Sinaloa and Zacatecas.

Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges of California south to northern Baja California, with isolated populations in southeastern California, southern Nevada and west-central Arizona; sea level to about 2,200 m.

Southern South Dakota, Nebraska, southeastern Wyoming and northeastern Colorado (northern segment); southern Colorado, southeastern Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas (southern segment); roughly 910-2,620 m. Not found in Canada.

Western North America from south-central British Columbia to northwestern Baja California, from the Pacific coast east to western Montana, Idaho, eastern Utah and north-central Arizona, to about 2,530 m.
Southwestern Washington (Willapa Hills) south through western Oregon to extreme northwestern California (Smith River watershed), from sea level to about 1,000 m.
Southwestern California south into northern Baja California, Mexico, from near sea level to about 2,290 m. Not found in Canada.

Under the Recuero et al. (2006) arrangement, from southern California, southern Nevada, southwestern Utah (possibly extirpated) and western Arizona south to southern Baja California; Recuero et al. did not give distributional details.

Large parts of Canada and the western and north-central US, from Great Bear Lake (Northwest Territories) and northern Ontario south to Arizona, New Mexico, northern Oklahoma, Missouri, Arkansas and Illinois, with disjunct populations in southern Ontario, southern Quebec, northern New York and northwestern Vermont; to about 3,670 m.

Southern British Columbia south through the western United States to southern Baja California, east to Montana, Idaho and Nevada; introduced populations on Haida Gwaii (Queen Charlotte Islands) and Revillagigedo Island, Alaska, and probably in desert California and Arizona. Montana populations are now attributed to the Sierran treefrog.
Central California, Nevada, eastern Oregon, Idaho and western Montana, possibly extreme northwestern Utah; genetic work (Jadin et al. 2021) found it, not the Pacific treefrog, in Idaho and Montana.

Southern California, southern Nevada and southwestern Utah south through Arizona, southern New Mexico and western Texas to southern Baja California and Colima, Mexico; from below sea level to about 1,520 m.

Northern California, southern Idaho, Utah, southeastern Colorado and southwestern Kansas south to central Baja California, Jalisco, San Luis Potosi and Tamaulipas; below sea level to about 1,900 m. Not found in Canada.

Southern and eastern California, western and southern Nevada and extreme southwestern Utah south through Arizona, southern New Mexico and southwestern Texas to the tip of Baja California, southern Sinaloa and Chihuahua; below sea level to about 2,135 m.
Southern Nevada, southern Utah, southeastern California and western Arizona south to southern Baja California and west-central Sonora, Mexico.

Central North America from southwestern Wyoming, Nebraska, southern South Dakota and Missouri south through eastern Colorado, eastern New Mexico, Kansas, Oklahoma and Arkansas to Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and southwestern Alabama. Not found in Canada.
Washington, Idaho, Montana and North Dakota south to northern Baja California, northern Arizona and northwestern New Mexico, east into western Nebraska; about 150-3,200 m. Not in Canada.
Nevada and southwestern Colorado south to northern Baja California, Sinaloa and Coahuila; west of the Central Valley in California and east to western Texas; near sea level to about 1,520 m.
Washington and southeastern Idaho south through Oregon, California, Nevada and western Utah to northwestern Baja California; sea level to about 3,350 m. Non-native in Montana.

From the north side of San Gorgonio Pass (Peninsular Ranges, southern California) south to near La Paz in southern Baja California, including several Gulf of California islands; sea level to about 2,130 m.

Southwestern Wyoming, eastern and southern Utah, western and south-central Colorado, northern and central Arizona and northern New Mexico; not in Canada. In Wyoming it is confined to the lower Green River valley and a narrow strip at the east edge of the Laramie Mountains.
California, Nevada, Arizona and Utah (Mojave, Great Basin and San Joaquin deserts); endemic to the United States, not in Canada.

Southwestern United States and northern Mexico: southeastern Oregon, southwestern Idaho, eastern California, western Nevada, southwestern Utah, western and southern Arizona, southwestern New Mexico and extreme western Texas. Not in Canada.

South-central Canada (southern Alberta and Saskatchewan, north to near Outlook, SK) south to north-central Mexico, west to western Montana, eastern Colorado and eastern Arizona and east to western Iowa, eastern Missouri and central Arkansas, with disjunct populations in southern Texas and Arkansas.

Southern British Columbia south through central and eastern Washington and Oregon, southern Idaho, eastern California, Nevada, Utah, Wyoming and northwestern Colorado to northwestern Arizona, from the Cascade-Sierra axis east to the Rockies.
Southeastern Utah, southern Colorado and northern Oklahoma south through Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas to Mexico (Guerrero and Oaxaca); up to about 2,470 m. Not in Canada.
Discontinuous from southern California, southern Nevada, Utah and west-central Colorado south to Arizona, southern New Mexico and Texas, and into northern Mexico. Not in Canada.

California Coast Ranges from east of Livermore and south of San Francisco Bay, through the Transverse Ranges, south to the tip of Baja California, reaching the desert side of mountains in southern California; not in Canada.

Pacific coast from Santa Cruz County, California, north to Juneau, Alaska, including Vancouver Island and other coastal islands, from sea level to about 2,740 m. Isolated populations in Latah County, Idaho and Saunders County, Montana; the Idaho population is probably introduced.

Southwestern Oregon and western California north of Point Conception (Coast Ranges from the Oregon border to central Santa Barbara County), from sea level to about 1,920 m; absent from the Salinas Valley. Not in Canada.
Sierra Nevada of California from the Pit and Sacramento rivers south to the Tehachapi Mountains, east along major rivers to the Owens Valley and west-central Nevada, about 90-2,440 m. Not in Canada.
Southern Colorado, southwestern Utah, central and eastern Arizona, New Mexico (except the far east) and western and central Texas, south through Mexico to Guatemala. Not in Canada.

Northern Mexico (Baja California) through the western United States, from New Mexico to western Oklahoma and Nebraska, the Dakotas and the Canadian border west to the Pacific Coast; in Canada, central and southern Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba.

Southwestern California, southwestern Arizona and southern New Mexico in the United States (abundant along the Gila and Colorado rivers), plus Mexico and Central America per Animal Diversity Web. Not in Canada.

Northern half of Humboldt County, California north through Oregon and Washington, east to the Cascades and west to the Pacific, and in Canada in southwestern British Columbia (Vancouver Island, Vancouver, north to Bella Coola).
Great Plains from the Oklahoma panhandle, northern Texas and northeastern New Mexico north to southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and east through Minnesota, Wisconsin and Indiana.

Across much of North America from Florida to coastal Quebec and west to British Columbia, south into southern California east of the Sierras and through the less arid Southwest (largely absent from the arid southwestern United States).

Southern Nevada (Nye County) and extreme southwestern Utah south through most of Arizona (except the northeast), southwestern New Mexico and southeastern California east of the Salton Trough to Sonora, western Chihuahua and northern Sinaloa. Not in Canada.

Southern California generally west of the Salton Trough (north to near Los Angeles on the coast and in the Mojave Desert to the Argus and Amargosa mountains) south through most of the Baja California peninsula and several Gulf of California islands.
Southern Nevada south into northeastern Baja California and northwestern Sonora, and from southeastern California east to northwestern and south-central Arizona. Not in Canada.

Extreme southern California (mountains of San Diego County north nearly to the Riverside County line) into Baja California, per the California account that treats U. microscutatus as part of this species.

Southwestern United States and northern Mexico: southeastern California, southern Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico and southwest/central Texas, south to Sonora, Sinaloa, Chihuahua and Coahuila. Not in Canada.

Arid western North America: central Washington and eastern Oregon south through the Great Basin, Nevada, Utah, Arizona and New Mexico to western Texas, plus central and southern California (north to San Francisco), Baja California and islands off the Pacific and Gulf of California coasts. Not in Canada.
Southern Utah, western Arizona, southern Nevada and southern California south to southwestern Sonora and Baja California. Not in Canada.

Appalachian Mountains from the Hudson River in New York to northern Alabama; NatureServe lists Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, North and South Carolina, Georgia and Alabama. Not recorded for Canada.
Southern Arizona through western Mexico to northern Nayarit, and Tiburon Island; sea level to about 1,500 m in Arizona.

Eastern US from southern Massachusetts and Rhode Island, through Connecticut and southeastern New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, to northwestern Georgia and Alabama and west to the Mississippi River; not recorded for Canada.

NatureServe lists it in the southeastern and south-central US, from New Jersey and Indiana south to Florida and west to Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas; Texas populations in SREL's account are a separate species (C. lineri). Not recorded for Canada.

Native from Italy across the Mediterranean and Middle East to Pakistan and North Africa; introduced and established in Mesa, Arizona (first confirmed 2007) and reported established in Florida, Britain and France. NatureServe lists only Arizona as exotic for the US.
Central Mississippi valley to the Gulf: NatureServe lists Illinois, Missouri, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama; not recorded for Canada.
Central Texas to southeastern New Mexico and south into Mexico; NatureServe lists Arizona, New Mexico and Texas. Not recorded for Canada.
Southeastern coastal plain: NatureServe lists North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana; not recorded for Canada.

Eastern and central US: NatureServe lists New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, Arkansas, Kentucky, West Virginia, Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi; not recorded for Canada.

Native from Egypt and the Middle East to western India; established through introduction in Texas (Galveston shipping docks), Arizona, California and Nevada (Center for North American Herpetology, citing SSAR); NatureServe lists Arizona and Texas as exotic.

Southeastern and south-central US coastal plain; NatureServe lists Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas; not recorded for Canada.

Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain: Virginia (to mid Mecklenburg County) and the North Carolina coastal plain per state agencies; NatureServe's narrower concept lists only Alabama and Florida. Not recorded for Canada.

Lowland drainages east of the Mississippi River, from extreme southern Illinois and southwestern Kentucky to east-central Tennessee and northwest Georgia, south to the Florida Panhandle and west through Alabama and Louisiana. Not in Canada.

Northeastern North America from southern New Brunswick and southern Quebec (and southeastern Ontario) south along the East Coast to North Carolina and west to Ohio, southern Indiana, Kentucky and Tennessee. Populations in southeastern Illinois and eastern Michigan are considered introduced.

Endemic to the eastern United States: from southwestern Pennsylvania southwest in the uplands through West Virginia, western Maryland, Virginia, eastern Kentucky, western North Carolina, eastern Tennessee, western South Carolina and northern Georgia. Not north or west of the Ohio River in the north. Not in Canada.

Ridge and Valley ridges of southwestern Virginia, the Cumberland Mountains and Plateau, and the Allegheny Mountains and Plateau from West Virginia north through Maryland, Pennsylvania, Ohio and New York, including the Adirondacks, to southern Quebec and southern Ontario.
Eastern Kentucky, adjacent southwestern Virginia, southern West Virginia and eastern Tennessee (Cumberland Plateau and Mountains). Not in Canada.
Southern Quebec and eastern Ontario south to northern Virginia, eastern West Virginia and central Ohio, with isolated populations in southern Labrador.
Illinois, Indiana, southern Ohio, western West Virginia and central Virginia south to northern Florida, southern Alabama, southern Mississippi and southeastern Louisiana. Not in Canada.

Virginia and Tennessee south through the Carolinas, Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi to the Gulf Coast, including eastern Louisiana and western Florida; absent from southern Georgia, most of peninsular Florida and high Appalachian elevations. Not in Canada.

Southern New York to Missouri, south to Arkansas, Tennessee, extreme northeastern Mississippi, northern Alabama, extreme northwestern Georgia, western North Carolina and northwestern Virginia. Not in Canada.
Coastal Plain from North Carolina to Lake Okeechobee, Florida, and west to eastern Texas. Not in Canada.
Coastal Plain from southeastern Virginia to southern Florida, west to eastern Texas and north in the Mississippi Valley to southern Illinois. Not in Canada.

Southern Maryland to southeastern Kansas and south to the Florida Keys, Gulf Coast and eastern Texas, with scattered disjunct northern and western populations. Introduced on the Bahamas and Grand Cayman. Not in Canada.

Southwestern Quebec, southern Ontario and northwestern Vermont to central Minnesota, south through the Mississippi drainage to Arkansas, northern Alabama and eastern Tennessee, west to eastern Kansas; Ohio River drainage; isolated populations in the Delaware, Susquehanna and Hudson drainages.
Endemic to the Pascagoula River drainage in Mississippi (Pascagoula, Leaf and Chickasawhay rivers and tributaries). Not in Canada.
Mississippi and St. Croix river basins from Minnesota and Wisconsin south through Louisiana, west to eastern Kansas, Oklahoma and eastern Texas, east into Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky. Not in Canada.

Mississippi and Missouri river basins from northern and central Wisconsin and Minnesota south through Louisiana and eastern Texas, west along the Missouri into North Dakota, east to western Tennessee, western Kentucky, Indiana and central Ohio. Introduced in southeastern Virginia. Not in Canada.
Mobile Bay drainage: eastern Mississippi, throughout Alabama and northwestern Georgia. Not in Canada.
Southern Quebec and southern Maine south through the Appalachians to northern Georgia, Alabama and northeastern Mississippi.

Discontinuously from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, southern Quebec and southern Ontario through Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota south to southeastern Oklahoma, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, the Florida panhandle and Georgia; fairly continuous in the northeast, spotty in the southwest.
Southern New England and southern Ontario to Minnesota and South Dakota, south to southern Texas, the Gulf Coast and southern Florida.

Southern Illinois and western Kentucky to the Gulf Coast from Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle, eastern Georgia and adjacent South Carolina, with disjunct populations in Louisiana, Arkansas and southeastern Oklahoma. Not in Canada.

South-central and southeastern US and areas west of the Great Lakes, from Manitoba, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, southern Ohio, West Virginia and Maryland south to eastern Texas, the Gulf Coast and northern Florida; exact boundary with gray treefrog is not precisely known.

Coastal Plain from Delaware to southern Florida and west to south-central Texas; north to southeastern Oklahoma, southeastern Missouri, southern Illinois and Indiana, western Kentucky and Tennessee and northern Alabama. Introduced in south-central Missouri, northwestern Puerto Rico and Brownsville, Texas. Not in Canada.
Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plains from southern Virginia to eastern Louisiana and south to southern Florida. Not in Canada.

Coastal Plain and some uplands from North Carolina to southern Florida and west to Louisiana, including northern Mississippi; disjunct populations in Delaware and Maryland, southwestern Kentucky and Tennessee and southeastern Virginia; introduced and probably extirpated in southern New Jersey. Not in Canada.
Coastal Plain and Mississippi Valley from southern Texas and southern Arkansas to southeastern Virginia and Florida; introduced on Grand Bahama. Not in Canada.

Southeastern Canada from southern Manitoba to New Brunswick, south through the northeastern and south-central US to North Carolina, West Virginia, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Illinois, Tennessee, eastern Texas and southwestern Louisiana, west to North Dakota, Minnesota, Iowa, eastern Kansas and eastern Oklahoma.
Southern Arkansas, southern Mississippi, Louisiana and central Texas in the United States, south to Veracruz, Mexico.
Arizona in the United States (NatureServe lists AZ only) and Sonora, Mexico.
South-central United States from Nebraska to southeastern Arizona, with an isolated population in Illinois-Iowa-Missouri; also northern Mexico.
Southern and central Arizona and southwestern New Mexico (Catron, Grant, Hidalgo counties), south into Sonora and Chihuahua, Mexico; considered extirpated from California.

Eastern United States from Long Island, New York south to the Florida Panhandle, west along the Gulf Coast to eastern Texas and north to southern Illinois and Indiana; disjunct population in northwestern Indiana.

Populations west of the Mississippi River across the plains states and east across the Mississippi embayment to Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, western Tennessee and northern Mississippi (NatureServe); the wider group reaches Maryland and Florida.
Eastern West Virginia, Maryland, Delaware and southern New Jersey south through the southeastern United States to southern Alabama.
Sierra Madre Occidental in eastern Sonora and western Chihuahua, north to the Madrean Sky Islands of southern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico.
Southeastern Virginia and the Coastal Plain of the Carolinas south through Georgia to southern Florida and west to eastern Louisiana, Tennessee and Kentucky.
Southern Minnesota, Michigan, southern Ontario, southern Quebec and southern Maine south to North Carolina and northern Alabama and Georgia; also Mississippi and northeastern Louisiana.

Extreme southern San Diego County (Tijuana and Otay watersheds), the Baja California peninsula and islands, Sonora, and isolated mountain ranges of western Arizona south of the Gila River (Maricopa, Pima, Pinal counties); sea level to 2,070 m.
Northern Mississippi, northern Louisiana and eastern Texas north through Oklahoma, Arkansas, western Tennessee and Kentucky to eastern Kansas, southern Illinois and Indiana (formerly southern Iowa).
Southern South Carolina to southern Florida and west to southeastern Texas; introduced in the Bahamas and northern Puerto Rico.

Coastal Plain from southern North Carolina (at least formerly) to northern Florida and west to southeastern Mississippi; most of the range is in northern Florida, southern Georgia and southern South Carolina.

Gaspe Peninsula of Quebec and New Brunswick/Nova Scotia west to Wisconsin and Missouri, south to South Carolina, northern Georgia, southern Mississippi and southeastern Texas; largely absent from Florida and southern Georgia.

Northern Alaska across boreal Canada to Labrador and south to New Jersey, northern Georgia and northern Idaho, with spotty distribution south to northern Colorado and disjunct populations in Arkansas-Missouri; extends farther north than any other North American amphibian.

Mississippi and Mobile drainage basins and the Gulf Coast from eastern Texas to the Florida panhandle, north to southeastern Kansas, southeastern Iowa, Illinois and southern Indiana; very rare in Kentucky and possibly extirpated in Indiana and Iowa.
Atlantic and Gulf coasts from Cape Cod to Texas.
Southeastern North Carolina to southern Florida and west to southeastern Louisiana, disjunctly north to central Alabama.

Gulf Coast drainages: western lineage from west-central Louisiana to northeastern and eastern Texas; other lineages from southeastern Louisiana to northeastern Mississippi and Alabama (Mobile Bay drainage).
Northern Louisiana north to Arkansas, eastern Oklahoma, southern Missouri and southeastern Kansas.
Southeastern Manitoba east to southern Quebec, south to Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York, northern Kentucky, southern Illinois, central Missouri and south-central Kansas.
Brackish coasts of the northern Gulf of Mexico from near Corpus Christi, Texas to Florida (including the Keys) and the Atlantic coast of northern Florida to Volusia County; also northern Cuba.
Coastal Plain from extreme western Florida and southern Alabama to southeastern Texas and north in the Mississippi Valley to southeastern Missouri and southern Illinois.

Southern Delaware and southeastern Maryland to northern Florida, west through Georgia and Alabama to southeastern New Mexico and western Texas, north to northeastern Kansas, western Missouri, central Illinois and southern Indiana; disjunct populations in Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Iowa and Illinois.

Southeastern United States: eastern Texas, southeastern Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, southeastern Missouri, western Tennessee, Mississippi, southern Alabama and Georgia, Florida and the Coastal Plain of the Carolinas. Not in Canada.
Concentrated in the Mississippi River drainage, north to southern Illinois and Indiana, west to Texas and Oklahoma (and Mexico), east into Alabama. Not in Canada.
Southern Ontario and the northeastern United States, from Nebraska and Kansas east to the Atlantic coast and south to North Carolina and southern Missouri.
Most of eastern North America, from the Canadian Maritime Provinces west to the Great Lakes and south to Texas, Alabama, Georgia and Florida.
Southeastern United States, north to southern New Jersey, through Florida to the Keys, west to central Oklahoma and Texas and into northern Mexico. Not in Canada.
Eastern and central United States, from the southern end of Lake Michigan and Wisconsin south through Texas and eastward to the Atlantic coast; Wisconsin populations are disjunct. Not in Canada.
Coastal Plain of the southeastern United States, including Florida, coastal South Carolina and coastal and southern Georgia; rare and poorly documented. Not in Canada.
Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plains: Florida, most of Georgia and South Carolina, coastal North Carolina and southeastern Virginia, west along the Gulf coast to eastern Louisiana. Not in Canada.
East of the Mississippi River to the Atlantic Seaboard Fall Line in Virginia, north to Wisconsin, Michigan, New York, Vermont, Massachusetts, and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
Southeastern United States from southern New Jersey to Florida and west through Mississippi to Louisiana; related Great Plains rat snake reaches Illinois, Texas and New Mexico. Not in Canada.
Central United States, north to southern Minnesota, south along the Mississippi River to the Gulf Coast; west to southern Nebraska and the eastern halves of Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. Not in Canada.

Throughout South Carolina and all but extreme northern Georgia (SREL); the wider range was not sourced in detail. Not in Canada.
Central and eastern United States, from Pennsylvania to Florida and Indiana to Texas. Not in Canada.
Southwestern Kentucky, western Tennessee, western Alabama, most of Mississippi and a small part of southeastern Louisiana, west of the Tennessee River on the Coastal Plain. Not in Canada.
Illinois and Indiana south to north and central Alabama, mainly in the Southwestern Appalachians and Interior Plateau uplands. Not in Canada.

Small, scattered populations in the southeastern Piedmont and adjacent areas: western South Carolina, west Georgia, central and east-central Alabama, south-central Mississippi and Louisiana. Not in Canada.
Appalachian Mountains from northwestern Pennsylvania to central Alabama, generally at elevations of about 365-1066 m. Not in Canada.
Eastern North America from southeastern Manitoba east to the Atlantic, south to eastern Texas and mainland Florida (not the Florida Peninsula, per Animal Diversity Web). Introduced in Cuba.

Southeastern United States: southeastern Missouri, northeastern Arkansas and eastern Mississippi east to coastal Virginia and the Carolinas, north to central and southern Pennsylvania, south to northern Florida. Not in Canada.

Southeastern coast of the United States: Florida, southern Georgia, eastern South Carolina and North Carolina (north to the Tar and Pamlico Rivers), west to southern Alabama and Mississippi, with a disjunct population in southeastern Virginia. Not in Canada.
Coastal Plain of the southeastern United States, absent from southern peninsular Florida. Not in Canada.

Eastern and central United States: northern Ohio south to northern Florida, eastern Virginia west to eastern Texas, with disjunct populations in the New River (VA/WV) and Tennessee River. Introduced in Europe (Spain) through the pet trade. Not native to Canada.
Southeastern United States from southern New York to northern Florida and from the Atlantic coast west to Kentucky and Tennessee. Not in Canada.

Eastern United States from New York south along the Appalachians to the Gulf Coast of Louisiana, Alabama and the western Florida panhandle; absent from the Coastal Plain of Virginia, the Carolinas and Georgia. NatureServe lists a Canadian national record (CA), but no Canadian range was sourced.
Central United States only, per NatureServe: Arkansas, Iowa, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Texas; not listed for Canada.

Southeastern United States, per NatureServe: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas and Virginia; in Florida from Osceola County northwest into the Panhandle.

Eastern United States from the southern Great Lakes to the Florida panhandle and east to the Carolinas, north to Pennsylvania and New York; in Canada only southern Ontario (Georgian Bay, Bois Blanc Island), ranked N2 and listed Endangered under SARA.

Southeastern coastal plain of the United States only: Alabama, Florida (most of the peninsula south to near Lake Okeechobee plus the central panhandle), Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina and South Carolina.
Southwestern United States (Arizona, California, Colorado, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas) into northern Mexico and Baja California; not found in Canada.
Eastern and southeastern United States from Massachusetts to Florida and west to the Mississippi River basin; absent from higher Appalachian elevations; not in Canada.
Southwestern United States: southern and eastern Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas (NatureServe also lists Navajo Nation) into northern Chihuahua; not in Canada.

Eastern United States (NatureServe: Alabama, Delaware, DC, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia); Animal Diversity Web gives the broader concept as mid New York to mid Florida and west to Colorado; not in Canada.

Eastern and central-eastern United States (NatureServe: Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, West Virginia) and northern Mexico; not in Canada.
Northern edge of a largely tropical range: southeastern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico in the United States (state rank S1, state-threatened in New Mexico), south to Costa Rica; not in Canada.

Southeastern United States; NatureServe lists Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia under the current name, while Animal Diversity Web's older concept runs from Virginia to Florida and west to eastern Texas and up the Mississippi drainage; not in Canada.

Southeastern and south-central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas; not in Canada.
South-central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Texas (Brazos River in Texas to the Pascagoula River in Mississippi); not in Canada.

Southeastern United States; NatureServe restricts the species to river drainages in Alabama, Georgia and Florida (Athens, Georgia south to near Orlando), while the broader older concept reaches central Florida north to Virginia and west to Louisiana; not in Canada.

Eastern and central United States from southern Maine, Michigan and Wisconsin to Florida and east Texas (absent from higher elevations); in Canada southern Ontario and Quebec (NatureServe rank N3; federally Special Concern).
Eastern United States (east of the Rockies) and northern Mexico; in Canada southern Ontario and Quebec (NatureServe rank N5).

Eastern North America: United States from eastern North Dakota and Wyoming (Black Hills) to the Atlantic and Gulf; in Canada Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island (NatureServe also shows Newfoundland as an exotic record).

Southeastern United States from North Carolina west to Louisiana, with an isolated population in Kentucky (Indiana also records it); generally absent from southern Georgia and peninsular Florida; not in Canada.

Native to northern and Saharan/sub-Saharan Africa. Introduced in the United States: Florida (known since the 1990s from scattered sites including Lee and Miami-Dade counties) and California (Redlands, San Bernardino County, since the early 2000s; San Juan Capistrano, Orange County, 2020); NatureServe lists it as non-native. Not in Canada.

Eastern United States from southern Maine to Florida and west to Michigan, Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. In Canada NatureServe treats Ontario as an exotic record and SARA lists the species as Extirpated.

Central United States (NatureServe: Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Texas, Wisconsin); Animal Diversity Web adds the range south through Mexico into Central America; not in Canada.
Eastern North America east of the Mississippi River from southern Maine and southern Ontario to Florida and Louisiana; in Canada Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia (NatureServe rank N4).
